summaries.summary: Abusive language is defined as insults, vulgarity, or profanity that debases targets, and is often reframed as offensive language, cyberbullying, othering language, and hate speech.
Increasing online harassment and offensive behaviors have led Facebook and Twitter to use multiple resources to censor offensive language, yet resolving the issue seems nearly impossible.
Abusive language detection fails because of subjectivity and context dependence, making human annotation laborious and large reliable datasets difficult to build.
Previous Twitter abusive language datasets ranged from 10K to 35K, while Hate and Abusive Speech on Twitter contains 100K tweets with cross-validated labels but no baseline reports.
This paper compares accuracy of machine learning classifiers and neural network models, presents reliable baseline results, and examines features, variants, and ensemble models.
Prior work applied Naïve Bayes, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Latent Dirichlet Allocation with word-level features to classify offensive language and offensive tweets.
Recent work applied distributed word representations and neural network models, including Continuous Bag Of Words, paragraph2vec, Gradient Boosted Decision Trees, and character-level representations.
Neural-based models with larger datasets have outperformed Logistic Regression and SVM, but no studies examine neural model efficiency with large-scale datasets over 100K.
This section details implementations of traditional machine learning classifiers, neural network based models, additional features, and variant models.
Five feature engineering based machine learning classifiers use BOW representations, TF-IDF normalization, word-level 1 to 3 n-grams, and character-level 3 to 8-grams.
Naïve Bayes (NB) is implemented as Multinomial NB with additive smoothing constant 1.
Logistic Regression (LR) is implemented as Linear LR with L2 regularization constant 1 and limited-memory BFGS optimization.
Support Vector Machine (SVM) is implemented as Linear SVM with L2 regularization constant 1 and logistic loss function.
Random Forests (RF) average probabilistic predictions of 10 randomized decision trees.
Gradient Boosted Trees (GBT) use tree boosting with learning rate 1 and logistic loss function.
Neural network based models evaluate Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), and variants on a larger dataset using pre-trained GloVe word-level features.
Kim's CNN baseline uses word-level filters [1,2,3] with ReLU and max-pooling, and character-level filters [3,4,5,6,7,8] with max-pooling and a 1024-dimensional fully-connected layer.
HybridCNN concatenates max-pooled outputs from word-level and character-level CNN and feeds the vector to a fully-connected layer for prediction.
All three CNN models use cross entropy with softmax as their loss function and Adam as the optimizer.
The bidirectional RNN baseline uses a GRU cell, 1 encoding layer, 50 dimensional hidden states, input dropout probability 0.3, cross entropy with sigmoid, and Adam.
Self-matching attention and Latent Topic Clustering (LTC) are investigated to improve RNN baselines by retrieving text sequences twice and extracting latent topic information.
Manual analysis found that replied-to or quoted tweets, called “context tweets”, provide significant contextual information and may help computers detect abusive language.
Example (2) is labeled abusive due to vulgar language, but its intention is better understood with context tweet (1).
Context tweet (1) says, “I hate when I'm sitting in front of the bus and somebody with a wheelchair get on.”
INLINEFORM0 (2) says, “I hate it when I'm trying to board a bus and there's already an as**ole on it.”
Context tweet (3) is important for understanding abusive tweet (4), especially in identifying the target of the malice.
Context tweet (3) says, “Survivors of #Syria Gas Attack Recount `a Cruel Scene'.”
INLINEFORM0 (4) says, “Who the HELL is “LIKE
Huang et al. used context tweet attributes to improve a baseline LSTM model, but their meta-information approach was limited by high data dependency.
To avoid data dependency, context tweet text sequences are converted to vectors and concatenated with labeled tweet outputs for CNN and RNN models.
Hate and Abusive Speech on Twitter classifies tweets into 4 labels, “normal”, “spam”, “hateful” and “abusive”, and 70,904 tweets were crawled from 99,996 tweet IDs.
Preprocessing replaces user IDs, URLs, and frequently used emojis with special tokens, and uses a segmentation library for hashtags.

Character-level representations use Zhang et al.'s method with one-hot encoded vectors over 70 character dimensions: 26 lower-cased alphabets, 10 digits, and 34 special characters including whitespace.
Training truncates TF-IDF vectors to the top 14,000 word-level and 53,000 character-level representations, while neural network models replace words appearing only once as unknown tokens.
Evaluation uses 10-fold cross validation averaged over 5 tries, random 85:5:10 splits, and weighted average precision, recall, and F1 scores for all four labels.
Neural network models are more accurate than feature engineering based models except LR, whose best model has the same F1 score as the best CNN model.
Among traditional machine learning models, LR is most accurate, followed by GBT and RF, while character-level representations improve F1 scores of SVM and RF only.
RNN with LTC modules has the highest accuracy score, but variants show no significant improvements, and character-level features significantly decrease CNN and RNN accuracy.
Context tweets generally have little effect on baseline models but noticeably improve several metrics, including CNN highest recall and F1 for “hateful” and RNN highest recall for “abusive”.

Character-level features reduce neural network accuracy for Hate and Abusive Speech on Twitter due to lack of labeled data and label imbalance, but help traditional classifiers using TF-IDF-selected elements.

Neural network variants suffer from data insufficiency but perform positively on “spam” (14%) and “hateful” (4%) tweets, with highest F1 scores 0.551 from RNN-LTC and 0.309 from CNN with context tweets.
The paper reports baseline accuracy of learning models and variants on Hate and Abusive Speech on Twitter, finding bidirectional GRU networks with LTC most accurate and suggesting ensemble models.
K. Jung is with Seoul National University, and the work was supported by NRF (No. 2016M3C4A7952632) and the Technology Innovation Program (10073144).
The authors thank Yongkeun Hwang and Ji Ho Park for helpful discussions and valuable insights.
